At resonance the two reactances cancel and the circuit behaves as a **pure resistance**.
**Step 1 — state the resonance condition.**
X_L = X_C
ωL = 1/(ωC), so **ω = 1/√(LC)** ✓
**Step 2 — find the impedance.**
Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)
= √(R² + 0)
= **R** ✓ its **minimum** possible value.
**Step 3 — find the phase angle.**
tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R = 0
**φ = 0** ✓
so the current and the applied voltage are **in phase** - which is the statement asked
for.
**Step 4 — check the other options against this.**
"**impedance is maximum**" ✗ - at resonance Z = R is a **minimum**; away from resonance
the reactive term adds and Z grows.
"**current is minimum**" ✗ - with Z smallest, the current I = V/Z is at its
**maximum** ✓
"**current leads the voltage by π/2**" ✗ - that describes a purely **capacitive**
circuit; at resonance the phase difference is **zero**.
**The sharpness of resonance.** The current peaks at ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and falls away on
either side ✓ How sharply is measured by the **quality factor** Q = ω₀L/R: a small R
gives a tall, narrow peak, a large R a broad, flat one.
**Why this is useful.** Tuning a radio means adjusting C until ω₀ matches the station's
frequency ✓ At that setting the circuit responds strongly to that one frequency and
weakly to all others.
**What happens either side of resonance.**
below ω₀: X_C > X_L, the circuit is **capacitive** and the current **leads**
above ω₀: X_L > X_C, the circuit is **inductive** and the current **lags** ✓
Resonance is precisely the crossing point, where neither leads.
∴ the current and voltage are in phase.

Find the rms current from the bulb's power rating, then multiply by √2 for the peak.
**Step 1 — find the rms current.** The bulb consumes 12 W at 48 V:
I_rms = P/V
= 12/48
= **0·25 A = 1/4 A**
**Step 2 — convert to the peak current.**
I₀ = I_rms √2
= (1/4)√2
= √2/4
= **1/(2√2) A** ✓
since √2/4 = √2/(2 x 2) = 1/(2√2) after rationalising.
**Step 3 — check the arithmetic numerically.**
1/(2√2) = 1/2·828 = **0·354 A**
and (0·25)(1·414) = **0·354 A** ✓ the same.
**Why the power formula uses rms values.** P = V_rms I_rms for a resistive load such as a
filament bulb ✓ The rms values are defined precisely so that this familiar product gives
the correct **average** power; using peak values would overstate it by a factor of two.
**Why a bulb counts as purely resistive.** A filament has negligible inductance and
capacitance, so the power factor is **1** ✓ That is what allows P = VI with no cos φ
term.
**The secondary's job here.** The transformer steps 230 V or so down to 48 V, and the
current it supplies is whatever the bulb draws ✓ The transformer's own turns ratio never
enters this calculation - only the output voltage and the load matter.
**The two forms of the answer.**
√2/4 = 0·354 A
1/(2√2) = 0·354 A ✓ identical, and recognising that they are the same expression is part
of this question.
**Reading the distractors.** **1/√2 = 0·707 A** ✗ is four times too large - it would mean
an rms current of 0·5 A and a 24 W bulb. **√2 = 1·414 A** ✗ is larger still. **1/4 A** ✗
is the **rms** current, not the peak - the commonest slip, since it appears in the
working ✓
∴ 1/(2√2) A.

The phase difference converts to a time lag by dividing by the **angular** frequency.
**Step 1 — find the phase angle.**
tan φ = X_L/R
= (1/√3)/1
= 1/√3
**φ = 30° = π/6 radians** ✓
**Step 2 — find the angular frequency.**
ω = 2πf
= 2π(50)
= **100π rad s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — convert the phase to a time.** A phase angle φ corresponds to a time
t = φ/ω
= (π/6)/(100π)
= 1/600
**t = 1/600 s** ✓
**Why φ/ω gives a time.** In a time t the phase advances by ωt ✓ so a phase difference φ
corresponds to t = φ/ω - the same relation that turns a full cycle, 2π, into the period
2π/ω.
**A check by fractions of a period.** The period is
T = 1/f = **1/50 s = 20 ms**
and 30° is a **twelfth** of a full 360° cycle, so
t = T/12 = (1/50)/12 = **1/600 s** ✓ confirming the answer without any π at all.
**Which lags which.** The circuit is **inductive**, so the **current lags the voltage**
by 30° ✓ Maximum voltage is reached 1/600 s = 1·67 ms before maximum current.
**Why the 200 V is not needed.** The phase angle depends only on the **ratio** X_L/R ✓
The supply voltage would be needed to find the current, but not the time lag - it is
given to see whether that is recognised.
**The impedance, for completeness.**
Z = √(1 + 1/3) = √(4/3) = **1·155 Ω**
so I_rms = 200/1·155 = **173 A** - a large current, since the impedance is only about an
ohm.
**Reading the distractors.** **1/300 s** ✗ is T/6, a 60° lag, which would need
X_L = √3 R. **1/200 s** ✗ is T/10, and **1/500 s** ✗ is T/4 - neither corresponds to a
standard angle from tan φ = 1/√3 ✓
∴ 1/600 s.

The power loss is **I²R** in the transmission line, so find the line current at the
**high** voltage and the total resistance of both wires.
**Step 1 — find the current in the line.** Power is transmitted at 45000 V:
I = P/V
= 900000/45000
= **20 A** ✓
**Step 2 — find the resistance of the line.** The current goes out along one wire and
returns along the other, so the length is **twice** the distance:
length = 2 x 20 km = 40 km = **40000 m**
R = 40000 x 5 x 10⁻⁴
= **20 Ω**
**Step 3 — find the power lost as heat.**
P_loss = I²R
= (20)²(20)
= 400 x 20
= 8000 W
= **8 kW** ✓
**Why transmission is done at high voltage.** The loss goes as **I²**, and for a given
power the current is inversely proportional to the voltage ✓ Transmitting the same
900 kW at **220 V** would need
I = 900000/220 = **4091 A**
and the loss would be (4091)²(20) = **335 MW** - vastly more than the power being sent.
Hence the step-up at the station and the step-down at the town.
**How small the loss is as a fraction.**
8 kW out of 900 kW = **0·9%** ✓ an acceptable figure, and typical of real transmission
lines.
**Why the line length is doubled.** A circuit needs a return path ✓ "Two-wires line"
means 20 km out and 20 km back, so 40 km of conductor carries the current.
**The voltage dropped along the line.**
V_drop = IR = 20 x 20 = **400 V**
out of 45000 V, under 1% ✓ consistent with the 0·9% power loss, as it must be.
**Reading the distractors.** **4 kW** ✗ uses only one wire's 10 Ω. **40 kW** ✗ and
**80 kW** ✗ are ten times too large, as if the current were 45 A or the resistance
200 Ω ✓ Checking that the loss is a small percentage of 900 kW rules both out at a
glance.
∴ 8 kW.

Bohr's radius scales as **n²/Z**, so a higher nuclear charge must be offset by a higher
quantum number.
**Step 1 — write the Bohr radius for a hydrogen-like ion.**
r_n = a₀ n²/Z
with a₀ = 0·529 Å the Bohr radius of hydrogen's ground state ✓
**Step 2 — identify Z for triply ionised beryllium.** Be has atomic number **4**, and
Be³⁺ has lost three electrons, leaving **one** electron around a nucleus of charge
**Z = 4** ✓ - a hydrogen-like ion, so the formula applies.
**Step 3 — impose the condition.** The orbit must match hydrogen's ground state, where
n = 1 and Z = 1:
a₀ n²/4 = a₀ (1)²/1
n² = 4
**n = 2** ✓
**Why a larger Z pulls the orbits in.** A nuclear charge four times greater attracts the
electron four times more strongly at the same distance, so every orbit shrinks by a
factor of Z ✓ To get back out to hydrogen's radius the electron must be promoted until
n² compensates - here to n = 2.
**The numbers.**
hydrogen, n = 1: r = **0·529 Å**
Be³⁺, n = 1: r = 0·529/4 = **0·132 Å**
Be³⁺, n = 2: r = 0·529(4)/4 = **0·529 Å** ✓ exactly hydrogen's ground-state radius.
**The general rule for hydrogen-like ions.** The radii match whenever
n²/Z is the same ✓ so He⁺ (Z = 2) would need n = √2, which is not an integer - no state
of He⁺ has exactly hydrogen's radius. Be³⁺ works because 4 is a perfect square.
**The energy, by contrast.** E_n = −13·6 Z²/n² eV, so for Be³⁺ at n = 2:
E = −13·6(16)/4 = **−54·4 eV** ✓ four times more tightly bound than hydrogen's −13·6 eV,
even though the radius is the same.
**Reading the distractors.** **n = 1** ✗ gives a quarter of hydrogen's radius. **n = 3**
✗ gives 9/4 of it, and **n = 4** ✗ four times ✓ Only n² = Z = 4 matches.
∴ n = 2.

Apply the Rydberg formula to the **first line** of each series.
**Step 1 — the first member of the Lyman series.** It is the n = 2 → 1 transition:
1/λ₁ = R(1/1² − 1/2²)
= R(1 − 1/4)
= **3R/4**
so **λ₁ = 4/(3R)**
**Step 2 — the first member of the Paschen series.** It is the n = 4 → 3 transition:
1/λ₂ = R(1/3² − 1/4²)
= R(1/9 − 1/16)
= R(16 − 9)/144
= **7R/144**
so **λ₂ = 144/(7R)**
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
λ₁ : λ₂ = (4/3R) : (144/7R)
= 4/3 x 7/144
= 28/432
= **7 : 108** ✓
**Why λ₁ is so much shorter.** The Lyman series ends on **n = 1**, the most tightly bound
level, so its photons carry the largest energies ✓ Paschen ends on n = 3, a shallow
level, so its photons are feeble and their wavelengths long.
**The actual wavelengths, with R = 1·097 x 10⁷ m⁻¹.**
λ₁ = 4/(3 x 1·097 x 10⁷) = **121·5 nm** - ultraviolet
λ₂ = 144/(7 x 1·097 x 10⁷) = **1875 nm** - infrared ✓
and their ratio is 121·5/1875 = **0·0648**, while 7/108 = **0·0648** ✓ exactly.
**Which series is which.** Every series is named by the level the electron **falls to**:
**Lyman** → n = 1, ultraviolet
**Balmer** → n = 2, visible
**Paschen** → n = 3, infrared ✓
and the **first member** of a series is always the transition from the next level up.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 3** ✗ and **1 : 30** ✗ are far too large a ratio - the
wavelengths differ by a factor of about 15, not 3. **7 : 50** ✗ has the right numerator
but the wrong denominator, from mis-evaluating 1/9 − 1/16 ✓ That subtraction, giving
7/144, is the one piece of real arithmetic here.
∴ 7 : 108.

The series whose lines fall in the visible is the **Balmer** series, the one ending on
n = 2.
**Step 1 — recall where each series lands.**
**Lyman** (to n = 1): 91 to 122 nm - **ultraviolet** ✓
**Balmer** (to n = 2): 365 to 656 nm - **visible** ✓
**Paschen** (to n = 3): 820 to 1875 nm - infrared
**Brackett** (to n = 4): 1460 to 4050 nm - far infrared
**Step 2 — check Balmer against the visible range.** The eye responds from about
**400 nm to 700 nm** ✓ and the first four Balmer lines are
H_α: 656 nm - **red** (3 → 2)
H_β: 486 nm - **blue-green** (4 → 2)
H_γ: 434 nm - **violet** (5 → 2)
H_δ: 410 nm - **violet** (6 → 2) ✓
all comfortably inside the visible window.
**Why Lyman is too energetic.** Falling all the way to n = 1 releases at least 10·2 eV,
giving photons of 122 nm or shorter ✓ Visible photons carry only 1·8 to 3·1 eV, so no
Lyman line can be seen.
**Why Paschen and Brackett are too feeble.** Ending on n = 3 or n = 4, their largest
transition energy is 1·5 eV or less ✓ below the red end of the spectrum.
**A worked check on H_α.**
1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/9) = 1·097 x 10⁷(5/36) = 1·524 x 10⁶
**λ = 656 nm** ✓ the familiar deep red line of hydrogen, seen in every discharge tube and
in the Sun's chromosphere.
**Where this is used.** The Balmer lines are the backbone of stellar spectroscopy ✓
Their presence, strength and Doppler shift reveal a star's temperature, composition and
velocity - all from transitions ending on n = 2.
**Reading the distractors.** **Lyman** ✗ is ultraviolet, **Paschen** ✗ and **Brackett**
✗ infrared ✓ Only one series has its photon energies in the 1·8 to 3·1 eV window the eye
responds to.
∴ Balmer.

Write the Rydberg formula for a transition ending on the **ground state** and rearrange
for n.
**Step 1 — write the formula.** The atom falls from level n to n = 1:
1/λ = R(1/1² − 1/n²)
= R(1 − 1/n²)
**Step 2 — divide through by R.**
1/(λR) = 1 − 1/n²
**Step 3 — isolate 1/n².**
1/n² = 1 − 1/(λR)
= (λR − 1)/(λR)
**Step 4 — invert and take the square root.**
n² = λR/(λR − 1)
**n = √[λR/(λR − 1)]** ✓
**A check on the limits.**
as n → ∞, 1/λ → R, so λR → 1 and the denominator → 0, making n → **∞** ✓ consistent
for n = 2, λ = 4/(3R), so λR = 4/3 and
n = √[(4/3)/(1/3)] = √4 = **2** ✓ exactly right - the formula reproduces the first Lyman
line.
**A second check, with n = 3.** The Lyman-β line has 1/λ = R(1 − 1/9) = 8R/9, so
λR = 9/8:
n = √[(9/8)/(1/8)] = √9 = **3** ✓
**Why λR must exceed 1.** The shortest Lyman wavelength is the series limit at
λ = 1/R ✓ Every real line is **longer** than that, so λR > 1 and the denominator is
positive - the expression is always well defined.
**The dimensional check.** R is in m⁻¹ and λ in m, so **λR is dimensionless** ✓ as it
must be, since n is a pure number. Options mixing λ and R without forming this product -
such as those with λR² or λ − 1 - fail this test immediately.
**Reading the distractors.** **√[λ/(λR − 1)]** ✗ and **√[λR²/(λR − 1)]** ✗ are not
dimensionless, so neither can equal an integer quantum number. **√[λR/(λ − 1)]** ✗
subtracts 1 from a **length**, which is meaningless ✓ Only one option is built entirely
from the dimensionless group λR.
∴ n = √[λR/(λR − 1)].
